name: Singer
title: Singer Sewing Machines: History, Models and Parts in the UK
description: Singer sewing machines in the UK: history since 1851, the famous Clydebank factory, vintage machines worth keeping, and parts and servicing.
intro: The most famous name in sewing, with a British story too: for nearly a century, Singer machines were made at Clydebank in Scotland.
cardText: History from 1851, Clydebank, vintage machines and parts.

sections.html: Isaac Merritt Singer and Edward Clark founded I. M. Singer & Co in the United States in 1851. Singer became one of the world’s first truly global brands, helped by instalment payments that let households buy machines over time.

Singer built a huge factory at Kilbowie, Clydebank, near Glasgow, in the 1880s. It became one of the largest sewing machine factories in the world and ran until 1980. The local railway station is still called Singer. That is why so many British homes still have a Clydebank-built Singer.

Older all-metal Singers, hand-crank, treadle and early electric models, are durable and repairable. Many sew straight stitch beautifully through heavy fabrics. Check the serial number to date your machine, and look for missing parts such as the bobbin case or shuttle before buying.

Today’s Singer range covers mechanical beginner machines, computerised models and heavy-duty machines. As with any brand, check the build, the buttonhole and parts availability for the specific model.

faqs.q: Is an old Singer worth repairing?
faqs.a: Often yes. Many older all-metal Singers are robust and parts for common models are still available. A specialist can check and service it.
